source.title: Interfacial fluoride engineering in layered sodium-ion cathodes: a computational screening and half-cell study
source.abstract: Sodium is roughly a thousand times more abundant in the Earth's crust than lithium, and sodium-ion cells are widely discussed as a cheaper route to stationary storage for household solar installations, which motivates the search for cathode materials that retain capacity over many charge cycles. Capacity fade in layered sodium transition-metal oxides is driven in part by irreversible reactions at the cathode-electrolyte interface. We screened 218 candidate fluoride surface terminations using density functional theory and selected four for synthesis. Coin half-cells were assembled and cycled at a rate of 1C. The best-performing termination retained 88% of initial capacity after 500 cycles, compared with 61% for the uncoated reference. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicates the formation of a thin sodium fluoride layer during the first cycle. We did not construct full cells, and half-cell results are known to overstate cycle life because the sodium metal counter-electrode supplies an unlimited sodium reservoir.
source.tldr: A fluoride surface coating improved capacity retention of a sodium-ion cathode from 61% to 88% over 500 cycles in half-cells.
